medical.title: Researchers lay out the case for integrating psychologists into primary health-care settings
medical.summary: As Prime Minister Mark Carney prepares to host the inaugural Canada Investment Summit in Toronto this September, a new review co-led by researchers at UBC argues that the country is leaving one of its largest economic and health care opportunities untouched: the integration of psychological care into primary care.

medical.title: Specific CAR T-cell subgroup could make lower-dose cancer therapy more effective
medical.summary: Immunotherapies strengthen the body's own anticancer defenses in a highly targeted manner. In therapies using so-called CAR T cells (chimeric antigen receptor T cells), a patient's immune cells are genetically engineered and directed against individual cancer cells. Until now, it has remained unclear why even very low CAR T-cell doses are effective in some patients while others do not benefit from the treatment.

medical.title: Dopamine-targeting treatments show only modest benefits for anhedonia, prompting calls for new research approaches
medical.summary: Dopamine has long been considered central to understanding anhedonia—the loss of pleasure, interest and motivation that is a common feature of depression and other mental health conditions. However, a new international expert report published in BMJ Mental Health suggests that dopamine alone cannot explain the condition and that future research must look beyond a single biological pathway.

medical.title: Regular ketamine infusions offer new hope for treatment-resistant bipolar depression
medical.summary: People living with treatment-resistant bipolar disorder still have options to manage their condition. However, the choices are often limited, may take weeks to work or fail to provide full relief. That has led to a search for faster, more effective alternatives.

medical.title: As probiotic use surges, microbiome-supportive food consumption stagnates
medical.summary: New research finds that probiotic supplement use has surged in the United States, while the consumption of microbiome-supportive foods has remained virtually unchanged.

medical.title: Beating 'mini-heart' derived from patient's blood cells offers personalized disease model
medical.summary: A team from the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Center (The Institute) have created a three-dimensional, beating heart-on-a-chip, or "mini-heart," using blood cells from a patient with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), a leading cause of heart transplantation. The new model could help researchers better understand the mechanisms underlying DCM, accelerate the evaluation of new treatments and, ultimately, explore the potential of patient-specific models to evaluate how an individual's heart tissue responds to different therapies. The study was recently published in Advanced Healthcare Materials.

medical.title: Transition to cleaner heating can lower blood pressure
medical.summary: An environmental policy designed to improve air quality also has benefits for cardiovascular health, a new McGill-led study finds.

medical.title: Major psychiatric risk gene linked to myelin and brain communication
medical.summary: A new Northwestern Medicine study suggests a major psychiatric risk gene remains important well into adulthood and may influence brain communication, according to a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

medical.title: Nearly one in five pediatric psychiatric crises involve digital media, new study finds
medical.summary: A new study analyzing more than 3,700 pediatric psychiatric crisis encounters at a large tertiary children's hospital finds that nearly 1 in 5 visits involved a digital media or device-related problem (DMRP), shedding light on an increasingly important but understudied factor in youth mental health emergencies.

medical.title: Vaccine protects against multiple fungal infections without hurting the gut
medical.summary: A vaccine created by University of Georgia researchers to battle multiple life-threatening fungal infections has successfully achieved protective immunity in preclinical animal models while maintaining the biodiversity of the gut microbiome, according to a new study published in Microbiology Spectrum.

medical.title: Distinct characteristics identified for patients with rheumatoid conditions, opioid use disorder
medical.summary: Patients with rheumatic conditions and opioid use disorder (OUD) have distinct demographic and clinical characteristics, including lower use of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and higher acute care use, according to a study published online July 13 in Arthritis Care & Research.

medical.title: Mouse study shows aging muscle leaves a molecular fingerprint in its supporting matrix
medical.summary: Aging is often described through what we can see and feel: weaker muscles, reduced mobility and slower recovery. But behind these visible changes are deeper biological shifts in cells, tissues and the molecular structures that support them. A recent study published in BMC Genomics offers a closer look at one of these hidden layers of aging: the extracellular matrix, or ECM, in skeletal muscle.

medical.title: FDA approves new pill for advanced breast cancer guided by blood test
medical.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a new daily pill for adults with advanced breast cancer whose tumors have found a way around their current treatment.

medical.title: Commonly used cancer drugs shown to boost MRSA antibiotics
medical.summary: Scientists at University of Galway have uncovered a link between commonly used anticancer drugs and antibiotics that could offer a new approach to tackling superbug infections. The research team set out to find new ways to treat methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections using drugs that are currently ineffective because of antibiotic resistance—a growing challenge in health care. MRSA is a type of S. aureus bacteria that has developed resistance to commonly used antibiotics, making infections more difficult to treat.

medical.title: Cash transfers to mothers with low income may slow biological aging in children
medical.summary: A study published in Nature Human Behaviour reports that providing cash transfers to low-income mothers during the first four years of their children's lives changed the children's biological aging in ways associated with better health in adulthood.

medical.title: Huachuma, the Andean psychedelic cactus, is drawing Western seekers and raising ethical questions
medical.summary: For at least two decades, thousands of Americans have been going to Peru, Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil to look for ayahuasca, a psychoactive brew traditionally used in sacred ceremonies in South America. Ayahuasca contains the psychedelic compound DMT, N,N-Dimethyltryptamine, and researchers are studying its effects on several conditions, including depression and addiction.

medical.title: Experimental study points to systemic sclerosis treatment
medical.summary: Investigators at Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University used an experimental drug to reverse the effects of systemic sclerosis, a serious autoimmune disease. The study, conducted in a laboratory, was published in JCI Insight.

medical.title: Brain vascular cells resist gene changes across neurological disease models
medical.summary: Even though Alzheimer's disease, the hereditary vascular disorder CADASIL, and traumatic brain injury are all associated with inflammation and changes in the brain's blood vessels, many vascular cells appear to retain their normal genetic programs during disease, reports a study from Karolinska Institutet published in Nature Communications.

science.title: Star-fingered toads use fingertip lobules to detect prey in murky water
science.summary: Surinam toads (Pipa pipa) are strange, flat frogs with minuscule eyes that live in the murky waters of the Amazon basin and carry their eggs on their backs. The way they catch prey is even weirder. They lie in wait with outstretched forelimbs until a small fish approaches, then snap open their jaws to create enough suction to draw the fish into their tongueless mouths and swallow it whole, all in a few hundredths of a second. But how do these frogs hunt in low visibility with poor vision?

science.title: New molecular magnet design boosts performance for ultrahigh-density data storage
science.summary: Researchers at The University of Manchester and the Australian National University have developed a new class of molecular magnets that combines the most successful features of previous designs, resulting in some of the strongest magnetic memory properties reported to date.

science.title: New iron-bearing compounds could store water near Earth's core
science.summary: Geochemical studies of volcanic rocks from Baffin Island, Canada, and Iceland suggest that some of the water dating back to Earth's formation may still be preserved deep within the planet. However, it has remained unclear which minerals could store such quantities of water under the extreme conditions of Earth's interior.

science.title: Climate change may erase 25 million hectares of kelp forests by 2050
science.summary: Climate change is driving rapid declines in seaweed forests globally, outpacing restoration efforts and undermining seaweed restoration as a viable carbon dioxide removal strategy, according to an essay by Karen Filbee-Dexter at the University of Western Australia and colleagues, published Sept. 8 in the journal PLOS Biology.

science.title: Study reveals another reason to save the world's trees
science.summary: All over the world, from Oregon's old-growth forests to Queensland's eucalyptus groves, creatures depend on trees for shelter. A new analysis from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign suggests that as the climate destabilizes, the world's trees may become an even more important respite. That's because the study finds trees everywhere buffer their animal tenants from temperature extremes. The work is published in the journal Forest Ecology and Management.

science.title: Why should we care if there aren't any squished insects on our windshield?
science.summary: This summer, you may have wondered why you are seeing so few insects squished on your car's windshield compared with a road trip several years ago.

science.title: Bear baiting in England became more common following Norman invasion, research reveals
science.summary: Bear baiting in England became more popular after the Norman Conquest in 1066, new research shows. The study by Cardiff University and the University of Nottingham brings together archaeological analysis of bear bones and archival records to show the prevalence of the animals in England and northern France during medieval times. The study is published in the journal Society & Animals.

science.title: Male beauty ratings reveal lower averages but an exceptional upper tier
science.summary: Women's faces are rated as more attractive than men's across cultures, age groups and sexual orientations. This effect, known as the "Gender Attractiveness Gap" (GAP), was recently demonstrated in a large-scale study led by the Max Planck Institute for Empirical Aesthetics (MPIEA) in Frankfurt am Main, Germany. A new article in Current Opinion in Psychology takes a closer look at the underlying data.

science.title: Study predicts large disparities in access to food, water and energy in 2050
science.summary: How will global access to food, water and energy evolve in coming decades? A new study coauthored by MIT researchers suggests the answers could be very different depending on region, resource and income.

science.title: Plants' response to rising CO₂ could put the brakes on dryland expansion
science.summary: Drylands are defined as regions where rainfall is low relative to the atmosphere's ability to draw water from soil and plants. Expanding boundaries of these regions are frequent concerns in climate change considerations. While they can support large populations and ecosystems, dryland expansion can worsen water scarcity, land degradation and desertification.

science.title: Heat waves inhibit antibiotic resistance in soils, but at a price
science.summary: Extreme heat waves disrupt life in soil. Soil bacteria that produce and resist antibiotics switch into survival mode, temporarily reducing the number of resistance genes. At the same time, heat and drought are causing significant damage to soils and ecosystems, especially in cold, wet regions such as the Netherlands. This is evident from a large-scale European study by soil ecologist Franciska de Vries (University of Amsterdam) and colleagues. The findings are published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

science.title: Arthropods inspire interdisciplinary solutions to global challenges, initiative shows
science.summary: Arthropods are small, but they could play an outsized role in tackling some of the world's biggest challenges.

science.title: Beyond the sea walls: Underwater archaeology reveals the hidden scale of ancient Mediterranean ports
science.summary: Trade routes and ports have shaped the history of human civilization, with the Mediterranean network among the most prominent and influential. Yet our understanding of its past is shaped largely by what remains visible on land rather than by the sea itself. Stone-built structures such as docks, quays and breakwaters give us important clues, but they do not always reveal the full picture.

science.title: New way to harness copper makes antibiotic-resistant bacteria and cancer cells more vulnerable
science.summary: University of Missouri researchers have discovered a new way to harness one of the body's natural defenses: copper. While copper is essential for life and helps power important biological processes, having too much of it can be toxic. To keep copper levels in balance, cells rely on specialized proteins that regulate where it goes and how much is present.

science.title: Quiet black holes with a stellar companion raise questions about how they form
science.summary: Active black holes are easy to detect. Their superheated accretion disks emit bright X-rays, and the jets streaming from their poles are easily seen at visible and radio wavelengths. But most stellar-mass black holes are inactive. They either drift through the galaxy alone or orbit a companion star without consuming its material. We can't observe inactive black holes directly. We can only observe their effects on nearby objects. We currently know of three such black holes thanks to the Gaia spacecraft.

science.title: Hubble and Webb find that far-out solar system objects 'remember' the past
science.summary: For the first time, scientists used the combined power of NASA's Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes to study some of the most far-flung bodies in our solar system, trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs). Some are the smallest and faintest ever directly seen. The researchers unexpectedly found fewer small TNOs than expected and that the colors of these bodies followed the same relationships as those of their larger family members.

science.title: Fresh laundry scent leads to higher spending on second-hand clothes, study finds
science.summary: The scent of fresh laundry in a store encourages people to spend more on secondhand clothes than the scent of citrus or the typical scent of secondhand clothes does. This is according to research by psychologists Matteo Perini and Jasper de Groot of Radboud University. The researchers suggest that this effect is linked to people's tendency to avoid pathogens.

science.title: Interstellar visitor 3I/ATLAS carries clues from the frozen outskirts of another star system
science.summary: UK astronomers have uncovered new clues about the origin of 3I/ATLAS—only the third known object from beyond the solar system ever spotted. In a new paper published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, researchers reveal that the comet formed in extremely cold conditions, far from any star.

science.title: Pumping antibiotics out: A new route to bacterial drug resistance
science.summary: Bacteria can survive antibiotics in several ways, including by pumping the drugs out of their cells before they can take effect. Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a previously unknown mechanism that allows the bacterium responsible for many cases of pneumonia and meningitis to export the antibiotic fosfomycin.

environment.title: Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra
environment.summary: This gallery displays a collection of 16 galactic images from Chandra and other telescopes. Astronomers put galaxies into three main categories: spirals like our own Milky Way, ellipticals that are older and likely the results of mergers, and irregulars that can encompass a wide range of galactic phenomena. All types are represented in this collection. Each galactic image contains X-ray data from Chandra combined with data from telescopes such as NASA’s Webb, Hubble, IXPE, Swift, and NuSTAR, and others both in space and on the ground. The post Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra appeared first on NASA Science .

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.title: Star-fingered toads use fingertip lobules to detect prey in murky water
mix_items.summary: Surinam toads (Pipa pipa) are strange, flat frogs with minuscule eyes that live in the murky waters of the Amazon basin and carry their eggs on their backs. The way they catch prey is even weirder. They lie in wait with outstretched forelimbs until a small fish approaches, then snap open their jaws to create enough suction to draw the fish into their tongueless mouths and swallow it whole, all in a few hundredths of a second. But how do these frogs hunt in low visibility with poor vision?

mix_items.title: Researchers lay out the case for integrating psychologists into primary health-care settings
mix_items.summary: As Prime Minister Mark Carney prepares to host the inaugural Canada Investment Summit in Toronto this September, a new review co-led by researchers at UBC argues that the country is leaving one of its largest economic and health care opportunities untouched: the integration of psychological care into primary care.

mix_items.title: Specific CAR T-cell subgroup could make lower-dose cancer therapy more effective
mix_items.summary: Immunotherapies strengthen the body's own anticancer defenses in a highly targeted manner. In therapies using so-called CAR T cells (chimeric antigen receptor T cells), a patient's immune cells are genetically engineered and directed against individual cancer cells. Until now, it has remained unclear why even very low CAR T-cell doses are effective in some patients while others do not benefit from the treatment.

mix_items.title: New molecular magnet design boosts performance for ultrahigh-density data storage
mix_items.summary: Researchers at The University of Manchester and the Australian National University have developed a new class of molecular magnets that combines the most successful features of previous designs, resulting in some of the strongest magnetic memory properties reported to date.

mix_items.title: Dopamine-targeting treatments show only modest benefits for anhedonia, prompting calls for new research approaches
mix_items.summary: Dopamine has long been considered central to understanding anhedonia—the loss of pleasure, interest and motivation that is a common feature of depression and other mental health conditions. However, a new international expert report published in BMJ Mental Health suggests that dopamine alone cannot explain the condition and that future research must look beyond a single biological pathway.

mix_items.title: Regular ketamine infusions offer new hope for treatment-resistant bipolar depression
mix_items.summary: People living with treatment-resistant bipolar disorder still have options to manage their condition. However, the choices are often limited, may take weeks to work or fail to provide full relief. That has led to a search for faster, more effective alternatives.

mix_items.title: As probiotic use surges, microbiome-supportive food consumption stagnates
mix_items.summary: New research finds that probiotic supplement use has surged in the United States, while the consumption of microbiome-supportive foods has remained virtually unchanged.

mix_items.title: New iron-bearing compounds could store water near Earth's core
mix_items.summary: Geochemical studies of volcanic rocks from Baffin Island, Canada, and Iceland suggest that some of the water dating back to Earth's formation may still be preserved deep within the planet. However, it has remained unclear which minerals could store such quantities of water under the extreme conditions of Earth's interior.

mix_items.title: Climate change may erase 25 million hectares of kelp forests by 2050
mix_items.summary: Climate change is driving rapid declines in seaweed forests globally, outpacing restoration efforts and undermining seaweed restoration as a viable carbon dioxide removal strategy, according to an essay by Karen Filbee-Dexter at the University of Western Australia and colleagues, published Sept. 8 in the journal PLOS Biology.

mix_items.title: Study reveals another reason to save the world's trees
mix_items.summary: All over the world, from Oregon's old-growth forests to Queensland's eucalyptus groves, creatures depend on trees for shelter. A new analysis from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign suggests that as the climate destabilizes, the world's trees may become an even more important respite. That's because the study finds trees everywhere buffer their animal tenants from temperature extremes. The work is published in the journal Forest Ecology and Management.

mix_items.title: Beating 'mini-heart' derived from patient's blood cells offers personalized disease model
mix_items.summary: A team from the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Center (The Institute) have created a three-dimensional, beating heart-on-a-chip, or "mini-heart," using blood cells from a patient with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), a leading cause of heart transplantation. The new model could help researchers better understand the mechanisms underlying DCM, accelerate the evaluation of new treatments and, ultimately, explore the potential of patient-specific models to evaluate how an individual's heart tissue responds to different therapies. The study was recently published in Advanced Healthcare Materials.

mix_items.title: Transition to cleaner heating can lower blood pressure
mix_items.summary: An environmental policy designed to improve air quality also has benefits for cardiovascular health, a new McGill-led study finds.

mix_items.title: Major psychiatric risk gene linked to myelin and brain communication
mix_items.summary: A new Northwestern Medicine study suggests a major psychiatric risk gene remains important well into adulthood and may influence brain communication, according to a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.title: Why should we care if there aren't any squished insects on our windshield?
mix_items.summary: This summer, you may have wondered why you are seeing so few insects squished on your car's windshield compared with a road trip several years ago.

mix_items.title: Bear baiting in England became more common following Norman invasion, research reveals
mix_items.summary: Bear baiting in England became more popular after the Norman Conquest in 1066, new research shows. The study by Cardiff University and the University of Nottingham brings together archaeological analysis of bear bones and archival records to show the prevalence of the animals in England and northern France during medieval times. The study is published in the journal Society & Animals.

mix_items.title: Nearly one in five pediatric psychiatric crises involve digital media, new study finds
mix_items.summary: A new study analyzing more than 3,700 pediatric psychiatric crisis encounters at a large tertiary children's hospital finds that nearly 1 in 5 visits involved a digital media or device-related problem (DMRP), shedding light on an increasingly important but understudied factor in youth mental health emergencies.

mix_items.title: Vaccine protects against multiple fungal infections without hurting the gut
mix_items.summary: A vaccine created by University of Georgia researchers to battle multiple life-threatening fungal infections has successfully achieved protective immunity in preclinical animal models while maintaining the biodiversity of the gut microbiome, according to a new study published in Microbiology Spectrum.

mix_items.title: Male beauty ratings reveal lower averages but an exceptional upper tier
mix_items.summary: Women's faces are rated as more attractive than men's across cultures, age groups and sexual orientations. This effect, known as the "Gender Attractiveness Gap" (GAP), was recently demonstrated in a large-scale study led by the Max Planck Institute for Empirical Aesthetics (MPIEA) in Frankfurt am Main, Germany. A new article in Current Opinion in Psychology takes a closer look at the underlying data.

mix_items.title: Study predicts large disparities in access to food, water and energy in 2050
mix_items.summary: How will global access to food, water and energy evolve in coming decades? A new study coauthored by MIT researchers suggests the answers could be very different depending on region, resource and income.

mix_items.title: Plants' response to rising CO₂ could put the brakes on dryland expansion
mix_items.summary: Drylands are defined as regions where rainfall is low relative to the atmosphere's ability to draw water from soil and plants. Expanding boundaries of these regions are frequent concerns in climate change considerations. While they can support large populations and ecosystems, dryland expansion can worsen water scarcity, land degradation and desertification.

mix_items.title: Distinct characteristics identified for patients with rheumatoid conditions, opioid use disorder
mix_items.summary: Patients with rheumatic conditions and opioid use disorder (OUD) have distinct demographic and clinical characteristics, including lower use of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and higher acute care use, according to a study published online July 13 in Arthritis Care & Research.

mix_items.title: Heat waves inhibit antibiotic resistance in soils, but at a price
mix_items.summary: Extreme heat waves disrupt life in soil. Soil bacteria that produce and resist antibiotics switch into survival mode, temporarily reducing the number of resistance genes. At the same time, heat and drought are causing significant damage to soils and ecosystems, especially in cold, wet regions such as the Netherlands. This is evident from a large-scale European study by soil ecologist Franciska de Vries (University of Amsterdam) and colleagues. The findings are published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.title: Arthropods inspire interdisciplinary solutions to global challenges, initiative shows
mix_items.summary: Arthropods are small, but they could play an outsized role in tackling some of the world's biggest challenges.

mix_items.title: Mouse study shows aging muscle leaves a molecular fingerprint in its supporting matrix
mix_items.summary: Aging is often described through what we can see and feel: weaker muscles, reduced mobility and slower recovery. But behind these visible changes are deeper biological shifts in cells, tissues and the molecular structures that support them. A recent study published in BMC Genomics offers a closer look at one of these hidden layers of aging: the extracellular matrix, or ECM, in skeletal muscle.

mix_items.title: Beyond the sea walls: Underwater archaeology reveals the hidden scale of ancient Mediterranean ports
mix_items.summary: Trade routes and ports have shaped the history of human civilization, with the Mediterranean network among the most prominent and influential. Yet our understanding of its past is shaped largely by what remains visible on land rather than by the sea itself. Stone-built structures such as docks, quays and breakwaters give us important clues, but they do not always reveal the full picture.

mix_items.title: FDA approves new pill for advanced breast cancer guided by blood test
mix_items.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a new daily pill for adults with advanced breast cancer whose tumors have found a way around their current treatment.

mix_items.title: Commonly used cancer drugs shown to boost MRSA antibiotics
mix_items.summary: Scientists at University of Galway have uncovered a link between commonly used anticancer drugs and antibiotics that could offer a new approach to tackling superbug infections. The research team set out to find new ways to treat methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections using drugs that are currently ineffective because of antibiotic resistance—a growing challenge in health care. MRSA is a type of S. aureus bacteria that has developed resistance to commonly used antibiotics, making infections more difficult to treat.

mix_items.title: Cash transfers to mothers with low income may slow biological aging in children
mix_items.summary: A study published in Nature Human Behaviour reports that providing cash transfers to low-income mothers during the first four years of their children's lives changed the children's biological aging in ways associated with better health in adulthood.

mix_items.title: New way to harness copper makes antibiotic-resistant bacteria and cancer cells more vulnerable
mix_items.summary: University of Missouri researchers have discovered a new way to harness one of the body's natural defenses: copper. While copper is essential for life and helps power important biological processes, having too much of it can be toxic. To keep copper levels in balance, cells rely on specialized proteins that regulate where it goes and how much is present.

mix_items.title: Quiet black holes with a stellar companion raise questions about how they form
mix_items.summary: Active black holes are easy to detect. Their superheated accretion disks emit bright X-rays, and the jets streaming from their poles are easily seen at visible and radio wavelengths. But most stellar-mass black holes are inactive. They either drift through the galaxy alone or orbit a companion star without consuming its material. We can't observe inactive black holes directly. We can only observe their effects on nearby objects. We currently know of three such black holes thanks to the Gaia spacecraft.

mix_items.title: Hubble and Webb find that far-out solar system objects 'remember' the past
mix_items.summary: For the first time, scientists used the combined power of NASA's Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes to study some of the most far-flung bodies in our solar system, trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs). Some are the smallest and faintest ever directly seen. The researchers unexpectedly found fewer small TNOs than expected and that the colors of these bodies followed the same relationships as those of their larger family members.

mix_items.title: Huachuma, the Andean psychedelic cactus, is drawing Western seekers and raising ethical questions
mix_items.summary: For at least two decades, thousands of Americans have been going to Peru, Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil to look for ayahuasca, a psychoactive brew traditionally used in sacred ceremonies in South America. Ayahuasca contains the psychedelic compound DMT, N,N-Dimethyltryptamine, and researchers are studying its effects on several conditions, including depression and addiction.

mix_items.title: Experimental study points to systemic sclerosis treatment
mix_items.summary: Investigators at Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University used an experimental drug to reverse the effects of systemic sclerosis, a serious autoimmune disease. The study, conducted in a laboratory, was published in JCI Insight.

mix_items.title: Fresh laundry scent leads to higher spending on second-hand clothes, study finds
mix_items.summary: The scent of fresh laundry in a store encourages people to spend more on secondhand clothes than the scent of citrus or the typical scent of secondhand clothes does. This is according to research by psychologists Matteo Perini and Jasper de Groot of Radboud University. The researchers suggest that this effect is linked to people's tendency to avoid pathogens.

mix_items.title: Interstellar visitor 3I/ATLAS carries clues from the frozen outskirts of another star system
mix_items.summary: UK astronomers have uncovered new clues about the origin of 3I/ATLAS—only the third known object from beyond the solar system ever spotted. In a new paper published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, researchers reveal that the comet formed in extremely cold conditions, far from any star.

mix_items.title: Brain vascular cells resist gene changes across neurological disease models
mix_items.summary: Even though Alzheimer's disease, the hereditary vascular disorder CADASIL, and traumatic brain injury are all associated with inflammation and changes in the brain's blood vessels, many vascular cells appear to retain their normal genetic programs during disease, reports a study from Karolinska Institutet published in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Pumping antibiotics out: A new route to bacterial drug resistance
mix_items.summary: Bacteria can survive antibiotics in several ways, including by pumping the drugs out of their cells before they can take effect. Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a previously unknown mechanism that allows the bacterium responsible for many cases of pneumonia and meningitis to export the antibiotic fosfomycin.

mix_items.title: Marine conservation collides with mining in Indonesia’s biodiversity-rich Moramo Bay
mix_items.summary: SOUTH KONAWE, Indonesia — A marine protected area in Indonesia’s Southeast Sulawesi province is home to a critically depleted population of humphead wrasse. The species presence helped the area gain its protected status, but mining permits overlap parts of the conservation zone and line its coast. mix_items.title: Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra
mix_items.summary: This gallery displays a collection of 16 galactic images from Chandra and other telescopes. Astronomers put galaxies into three main categories: spirals like our own Milky Way, ellipticals that are older and likely the results of mergers, and irregulars that can encompass a wide range of galactic phenomena. All types are represented in this collection. Each galactic image contains X-ray data from Chandra combined with data from telescopes such as NASA’s Webb, Hubble, IXPE, Swift, and NuSTAR, and others both in space and on the ground. mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

satire_ro.title: Au dispărut toți cerșetorii din fața vilei lui Becali, de frică să nu fie puși antrenori la FCSB
